title: What is cloud computing? (on-demand infrastructure)
hook: Cloud computing means renting compute, storage, and networking over the internet instead of buying servers upfront. Amazon Web Services (AWS) lets you provision resources in minutes and pay only for what you use.

blocks.text: Cloud computing delivers Information Technology (IT) resources — virtual machines, databases, object storage, load balancers — as metered services over a network. Instead of capital expenditure on hardware and data centers, you use operational expenditure: spin up an Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instance when traffic spikes, scale down when it drops. AWS operates Regions (geographic areas) divided into Availability Zones (isolated data centers) so you can design for resilience without owning physical racks.

entries.plainDefinition: You manage operating systems and apps; the cloud provider manages physical hardware and virtualization.
entries.example: EC2 gives you a virtual server; you patch the guest operating system.

entries.plainDefinition: The provider manages runtime and infrastructure; you deploy application code.
entries.example: Elastic Beanstalk or AWS Lambda abstracts server management.

entries.plainDefinition: Fully managed application delivered over the internet.
entries.example: Amazon WorkMail is email as a service.

entries.plainDefinition: A geographic area with multiple isolated Availability Zones.
entries.example: us-east-1 (N. Virginia) is a common default Region.

blocks.text: Interviewers expect you to explain why companies moved from on-premises data centers to AWS: elasticity (scale in minutes), global reach (deploy closer to users), and shifting undifferentiated heavy lifting (power, cooling, hardware refresh) to AWS. You still own architecture, security configuration, and cost discipline — cloud is not magic cost savings without governance.

blocks.title: Interview framing
blocks.body: Contrast capex (buy servers) with opex (pay per hour). Name elasticity and Regions/AZs as the resilience building blocks.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Choose a Region
items.body: Pick geography for latency, compliance, and service availability.

items.title: Call the AWS API
items.body: Use console, Command Line Interface (CLI), or Infrastructure as Code (IaC) to create resources.

items.title: AWS provisions capacity
items.body: Hypervisor, storage, and network are allocated in seconds to minutes.

items.title: Metering starts
items.body: Billing tracks usage per second, per gigabyte, or per request depending on service.

snippet.label: CLI: list Regions and describe an instance
snippet.code:
aws ec2 describe-regions --query 'Regions[].RegionName' --output table

aws ec2 run-instances \
  --image-id ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 \
  --instance-type t3.micro \
  --subnet-id subnet-0abc123 \
  --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Environment,Value=dev}]'
snippet.explanation: describe-regions shows where you can deploy. run-instances provisions IaaS compute in a chosen subnet with tags for cost tracking.

snippet.label: CloudFormation: minimal EC2 stack
snippet.code:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Single dev EC2 instance
Resources:
  DevInstance:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Instance
    Properties:
      InstanceType: t3.micro
      ImageId: ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0
      Tags:
        - Key: Environment
          Value: dev
snippet.explanation: CloudFormation declares desired state. AWS creates the instance and tracks it as a stack resource for repeatable deployments.

snippet.label: CLI: check service quotas
snippet.explanation: Even on-demand cloud has limits. Quotas cap how many instances you can run per Region until you request an increase.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Calling cloud 'cheaper' without mentioning idle capacity and data transfer costs. Ignoring Region choice until compliance blocks a deployment. Treating SaaS and IaaS as interchangeable — they shift different layers of responsibility.

interviewTakeaways: Cloud computing delivers metered IT resources over the network with elasticity and global Regions.
IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS shift different management layers — know which AWS service fits each.
Tag resources at creation; untagged dev instances are a common surprise bill.
60s: Cloud is opex and elasticity. AWS Regions and AZs give geographic and fault isolation. You still own architecture, security config, and cost governance.
Follow-up: how do Availability Zones differ from Regions?
commonPitfalls: Saying cloud is always cheaper — saying that gets you rejected because idle capacity and egress fees often dominate.
Strong answer: cloud trades capex for opex and speed; cost discipline requires tagging, rightsizing, and architecture choices.
Deploying production in a Region without checking data residency requirements.
Confusing PaaS (Lambda) with IaaS (EC2) when discussing patching responsibility.

jsTsCorrelations.note: A Node.js app on EC2 is IaaS — you manage the process and OS. AWS Lambda is PaaS — you upload a handler function and AWS manages the runtime container lifecycle.
